must.text: Main diagnosis: the preferred leader of a partition is the first broker in its replica list; the script put broker 4 first in most lists, so broker 4 is the preferred leader of those partitions and leadership is already where Kafka wants it.

Explains that the automatic leader rebalance and kafka-leader-election --election-type preferred only move leadership to the preferred replica, so with this replica order they have nothing to do ('Valid replica already elected').

Fix: run a new reassignment (kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --execute with a JSON file) that keeps each partition's replica set but reorders the lists so that the first replica is spread evenly over the six brokers.

Moves leadership onto the new first replicas with a preferred leader election (kafka-leader-election.sh --election-type preferred), or relies on the automatic leader rebalance (auto.leader.rebalance.enable=true) to do it.

must_not.near_miss: Stopping broker 4 would move its leaders only until the automatic rebalance returns them to their preferred replica.

reference:
Nothing is stuck: leadership is exactly where Kafka wants it. The preferred leader of a partition is the first broker in its replica list, and your script put broker 4 first for most partitions (partition 0 is 4,1,5, partition 1 is 4,2,6, partition 3 is 4,3,6). Every partition is already led by its preferred replica, so the automatic rebalance (auto.leader.rebalance.enable) and kafka-leader-election --election-type preferred have nothing to do: both only move leadership back to the preferred replica, hence 'Valid replica already elected'.

Change the order, not the leader:
1. Write a reassignment JSON for orders-events (and every other topic the script touched) that keeps the same three brokers per partition but rotates the lists so each broker is first for two of the twelve partitions, for example partition 0 [1,4,5], partition 1 [2,4,6], partition 3 [3,4,6].
2. Run kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server ... --reassignment-json-file reorder.json --execute.
3. Run the same command with --verify until it reports completion.
4. Then run kafka-leader-election.sh --election-type preferred --all-topic-partitions, or wait for the automatic check (leader.imbalance.check.interval.seconds), so leaders move to the new first replicas.
5. Fix the script so it rotates the first replica.

Do not restart broker 4 to push leaders away (they come back with the next rebalance) and do not use an unclean election; all replicas are in sync.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Kafka treats the first replica in each list as the preferred leader. Your generator listed broker 4 first in most partitions, so broker 4 is supposed to lead them, and both the background rebalance and a manual preferred election leave things as they are: they only restore leadership to the preferred replica. To spread the load, generate a new plan that keeps the replica sets and only changes their order (round-robin the first position over brokers 1 to 6), apply it with kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --execute, confirm with --verify, and then let auto.leader.rebalance.enable or kafka-leader-election.sh --election-type preferred move the leaders onto the new first replicas. Afterwards kafka-topics --describe should show Leader equal to the first entry of Replicas, spread over all six brokers.
generic: Leader imbalance after adding brokers is common. Make sure auto.leader.rebalance.enable is true and lower leader.imbalance.check.interval.seconds. Run a preferred leader election with kafka-leader-election.sh and consider Cruise Control to balance load. Watch the network and request handler metrics of broker 4 and add brokers or bandwidth if it stays overloaded.
note: No any_of: the only documented fix is reordering the replica lists. Strimzi's tuning page names leader.imbalance.per.broker.percentage, which the 4.3 broker reference does not list; no point rests on it. Cruise Control (Strimzi) would also produce a balanced order but the cluster here is not on Strimzi.

must.text: Main diagnosis: max.decompressed.message.bytes caps the decompressed size of a single record and is enforced where the broker decompresses records, including log compaction and timestamp offset lookups; set below the size of records already stored (1.2-4 MB PDFs), it makes compaction and timestamp lookups of those partitions fail until it is raised again.

Explains that it is not the same limit as max.message.bytes: max.message.bytes bounds the compressed batch on the wire, max.decompressed.message.bytes bounds one record after decompression, so 'matching' the two cuts compressed records that were fine before.

Raise the cluster-wide value again: delete the dynamic default (kafka-configs.sh --entity-type brokers --entity-default --alter --delete-config max.decompressed.message.bytes) or set it above the largest stored record (more than 4 MB).

Or keep the cluster cap and set a topic-level max.decompressed.message.bytes on customer-documents above its largest record (for example 5242880) with kafka-configs.sh --entity-type topics --alter --add-config.
Explains the upload errors: new compressed batches holding a record above the cap are rejected at produce validation with InvalidRecordException (INVALID_RECORD); the same change fixes them.

must_not.condition: only if presented as the fix or as needed for it; saying these are not the cause does not count
must_not.near_miss: max.message.bytes bounds the compressed batch and is not what blocks compaction here.

must_not.text: Recommends deleting and recreating customer-documents, or deleting its records, to get compaction going again.
must_not.condition: only if recommended; naming it as what not to do does not count
must_not.near_miss: Once the cap is raised above the stored records, compaction and timestamp lookups work again; no data has to be removed.

reference:
The hardening change caused all three symptoms. max.decompressed.message.bytes (new in 4.2) caps the size of a single record after decompression, and the broker enforces it wherever it decompresses: produce validation of compressed batches, log compaction, and offset lookups by timestamp. Your PDFs are 1.2 to 4 MB once decompressed, so with a 1 MB cap:
- the log cleaner cannot compact the partitions of customer-documents (uncleanable-partitions-count 6, the topic keeps growing);
- timestamp offset lookups on those partitions fail, which breaks the replay job;
- new uploads with a record above 1 MB are rejected with InvalidRecordException (INVALID_RECORD).
The documentation says lowering the cap below already-stored records makes compaction and timestamp lookups fail until it is raised again.

It was never meant to match max.message.bytes: that one bounds the compressed batch on the wire, which your zstd batches still fit; this one bounds each record after decompression.

Fix: remove the dynamic cluster default so the broker falls back to the default (no practical limit):
kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --entity-type brokers --entity-default --alter --delete-config max.decompressed.message.bytes
or set it above your largest record, e.g. 8388608. Then watch uncleanable-partitions-count go back to 0, rerun the replay job and retry the failed uploads. Do not touch max.message.bytes and do not recreate the topic.
correct_alternative: If the security team wants to keep a 1 MB per-record cap for other topics, keep the cluster default and give customer-documents its own limit: kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --entity-type topics --entity-name customer-documents --alter --add-config max.decompressed.message.bytes=5242880. The topic-level setting overrides the cluster default. Reason: max.decompressed.message.bytes bounds a single record after decompression and is checked at produce validation, during log compaction and for timestamp offset lookups; with 1.2 to 4 MB PDFs under a 1 MB cap the cleaner cannot compact the partitions, the replay job's timestamp lookups fail, and new large documents are rejected with InvalidRecordException. It is not the same as max.message.bytes, which limits the compressed batch. After the override, check that uncleanable-partitions-count returns to 0 and retry the failed uploads.
generic: Large messages need matching limits on the producer, broker and consumer. Check max.message.bytes on the topic, message.max.bytes on the brokers, max.request.size on the producer and fetch.max.bytes on consumers. For documents of several megabytes, consider storing them in object storage and sending only a reference through Kafka. Also check log cleaner threads and disk space.
note: The uncleanable-partitions-count jump is inferred behaviour: the docs say compaction fails, not how the cleaner reports it. Whether the cleaner retries the partitions by itself after the cap is raised is not documented.

Verifies the fix: ISR back to all three replicas and the UnderReplicatedPartitions metric (or kafka-topics --describe --under-replicated-partitions) back to zero/empty.

must_not.condition: only if recommended as the fix; the cluster holds data the teams want to keep; saying a reformat is not needed does not count
must_not.near_miss: kafka-configs.sh can create SCRAM credentials after the brokers are started, so no reformat is needed.

must_not.text: Recommends lowering min.insync.replicas to 1 or keeping producers on acks=1 as the fix.
must_not.condition: only if recommended as the fix or workaround; describing what acks=1 does now does not count
must_not.near_miss: acks=1 does not help: the records stay invisible to consumers until they reach the ISR and min.insync.replicas is met.

reference:
The password is fine; the mechanism is not. SCRAM credentials are stored per mechanism: you formatted storage with a SCRAM-SHA-256 credential for admin (kafka-configs --describe shows only SCRAM-SHA-256), but sasl.mechanism.inter.broker.protocol is SCRAM-SHA-512. Every follower fetch authenticates as admin with SCRAM-SHA-512, finds no credential and fails ('invalid credentials with SASL mechanism SCRAM-SHA-512'), so the followers drop out of the ISR and every partition is down to its leader.

That explains the producers: with acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2 the leader rejects writes with NotEnoughReplicas. With acks=1 the leader accepts the write, but records are not visible to consumers until they are replicated to the ISR and min.insync.replicas is met, so consumers see nothing.

Fix (keeps the data): make the brokers use the mechanism the credential exists for. On each broker set sasl.mechanism.inter.broker.protocol=SCRAM-SHA-256 and the matching listener.name.sasl_ssl.scram-sha-256.sasl.jaas.config with username admin, then restart the brokers one at a time. The followers authenticate, catch up and rejoin the ISR.

Check: kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions returns nothing, UnderReplicatedPartitions is 0, and an acks=all producer succeeds and a consumer sees the records.

Do not reformat storage (it would delete the teams' data) and do not lower min.insync.replicas or move producers to acks=1.
correct_alternative:
Keep SCRAM-SHA-512 between brokers and create the credential that is missing. SCRAM credentials are per mechanism; admin only has SCRAM-SHA-256, created at format time, so inter-broker connections with SCRAM-SHA-512 fail and the followers leave the ISR. Using an admin client configured for SCRAM-SHA-256 (which works on this listener):
kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9093 --command-config admin-256.properties --alter --add-config 'SCRAM-SHA-512=[password=<same password>]' --entity-type users --entity-name admin
kafka-configs --describe should then list both mechanisms. The followers' fetchers retry, authenticate, catch up and rejoin the ISR; if not, restart the brokers one at a time. That also ends NotEnoughReplicas for acks=all, and records written with acks=1 become visible once they are replicated and min.insync.replicas is met. Confirm with --under-replicated-partitions (empty). No reformat and no change of min.insync.replicas.
generic: SASL authentication failures usually mean a wrong password or JAAS configuration. Check the JAAS file and that the user exists, make sure the clocks are in sync and that TLS certificates are valid. Check the ISR with kafka-topics --describe and look at the broker logs for replication errors. Restart the brokers after fixing the configuration.
note: The docs say inter-broker credentials 'must be created before Kafka brokers are started' but also that kafka-configs.sh creates credentials after start; that a running broker's fetchers recover once the SCRAM-SHA-512 credential is added is inferred, not documented (the alternative allows a rolling restart). The log prefixes in the evidence are invented; the message bodies are exact client strings. Second review: the evidence gained the server-side SCRAM-SHA-256 JAAS entry that authentication-using-sasl.md:37 requires when two mechanisms are enabled on a listener.

must.text: Main diagnosis: by default an Application is refreshed every time a resource it tracks changes, so the annotation writes on 2,400 KafkaTopics every five minutes drive continuous refreshes and the controller's CPU; the ignore rule meant to stop this is not taking effect.
resource.ignoreResourceUpdatesEnabled: "false" switches ignoring of resource updates off, so the ignoreResourceUpdates rule does nothing; set it to "true" or remove the key (true is the default).

The JSON pointer must escape the '/' inside the annotation key as ~1: /metadata/annotations/finops.example.com~1bytes-last-hour (or use jqPathExpressions with .metadata.annotations."finops.example.com/bytes-last-hour").
Verifies the fix in the application-controller log at debug level: the line 'Ignoring change of object because none of the watched resource fields have changed' appears for the KafkaTopic updates.

must_not.near_miss: timeout.reconciliation sets how often Argo CD checks Git; refreshes caused by resource updates are controlled by ignoreResourceUpdates.

must_not.text: Recommends removing the KafkaTopics from Argo CD management (deleting them from Git or from the Applications, or deleting the Applications) to stop the load.
must_not.condition: only if recommended; with pruning or cascading deletion the KafkaTopic resources are deleted and the Topic Operator then deletes the Kafka topics
must_not.near_miss: Ignoring only the annotation keeps the KafkaTopics managed and drift detection on spec intact.

reference:
Two mistakes in the customization, on top of the default behaviour. By default Argo CD refreshes an Application every time a resource it tracks changes; your FinOps job changes 2,400 tracked KafkaTopics every five minutes, which is the refresh storm in the log.

1. resource.ignoreResourceUpdatesEnabled: "false" turns ignoring of resource updates off, so no ignoreResourceUpdates rule is used. Remove the key or set it to "true" (the default).
2. The pointer is wrong: in a JSON pointer a '/' inside a key must be written as ~1. Use

data:
  resource.customizations.ignoreResourceUpdates.kafka.strimzi.io_KafkaTopic: |
    jsonPointers:
    - /metadata/annotations/finops.example.com~1bytes-last-hour

This only tells the controller not to refresh on changes to that field. It does not change diffing, so changes to spec in Git or in the cluster are still detected.

Check: in the application-controller log the 'Requesting app refresh caused by object update' lines for kind=KafkaTopic should stop and, at debug log level, 'Ignoring change of object because none of the watched resource fields have changed' should appear. CPU should fall within minutes.

Do not raise timeout.reconciliation (that is Git polling) and do not take the topics out of Argo CD: pruning or deleting the KafkaTopics makes the Topic Operator delete the topics.
correct_alternative:
Fix the flag first: resource.ignoreResourceUpdatesEnabled: "false" disables every ignore-updates rule, so remove it (the default is true). Then express the path with jq, which avoids pointer escaping:

resource.customizations.ignoreResourceUpdates.kafka.strimzi.io_KafkaTopic: |
  jqPathExpressions:
  - '.metadata.annotations."finops.example.com/bytes-last-hour"'

Why: every update of a tracked resource refreshes its Application by default; with the rule active the controller skips updates that only touch that annotation. If you prefer, the same jq expression can go into a system-level ignoreDifferences customization for the KafkaTopic kind, because Argo CD adds system-level ignoreDifferences to the ignored updates by default. Confirm with the controller's debug-level log line 'Ignoring change of object because none of the watched resource fields have changed'. Drift detection on spec is unaffected.
generic: High CPU on the application controller usually comes from too many Applications or resources. Increase the controller's CPU and memory, enable controller sharding, raise the status and operation processors, and consider increasing the reconciliation timeout. You can also reduce the number of Applications by grouping topics.
note: No any_of: the alternative uses the jq form, which m3 accepts. The annotation-writing FinOps job is invented. Argo CD's documented note: an ignored update still causes a refresh if the resource's health changes. That 'argocd admin settings resource-overrides ignore-resource-updates' can test the rule is in the commands reference, which is not indexed; no point rests on it.

Makes the broker principal (User:kafka-broker) a super user on the controllers as well (or grants it ClusterAction on the Cluster), because the controller authorizes the forwarded Envelope request with the broker's own principal.
super.users entries are separated by semicolons, not commas: super.users=User:kafka-broker;User:platform-admin.

With the default allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=false a resource without ACLs is open only to super users, so ACLs for each service principal (e.g. Write on topic orders for User:orders-svc) must exist before the services are switched over.
Creates the service ACLs through the cluster with kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server (or --bootstrap-controller) instead of the runbook's --authorizer-properties zookeeper.connect=... form.

reference:
Five changes.

1. Authorizer class: KRaft uses org.apache.kafka.metadata.authorizer.StandardAuthorizer, which keeps ACLs in the metadata log. Set it on all nodes:
authorizer.class.name=org.apache.kafka.metadata.authorizer.StandardAuthorizer
2. Controllers need it too. Admin requests such as CreateTopics go to a broker, which forwards them to the active controller in an Envelope request, and the controller authorizes them. The controller first authorizes the Envelope with the broker's principal (Envelope needs ClusterAction on the Cluster), then the request with the client's principal. So on the controllers add the authorizer, super.users including User:kafka-broker, and the same ssl.principal.mapping.rules so the broker certificate maps to that name.
3. super.users is semicolon-separated (SSL names may contain commas):
super.users=User:kafka-broker;User:platform-admin
4. Drop allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true. With the default (false) a resource without ACLs is open only to super users; with true, every authenticated principal can use any topic nobody wrote ACLs for.
5. ACLs are created through the cluster, not ZooKeeper: --authorizer-properties was removed in 4.0.
kafka-acls.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9093 --command-config admin.properties --add --allow-principal User:orders-svc --operation Write --topic orders
Create the ACLs for every service before it is switched to the cluster; otherwise its requests are denied.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Replace the class with org.apache.kafka.metadata.authorizer.StandardAuthorizer, the authorizer for KRaft clusters, and put it on every node, controllers included: brokers forward admin requests to the active controller, which authorizes them. The controller checks the forwarding broker's principal for ClusterAction on the Cluster (Envelope), so User:kafka-broker must be a super user there too, with the same CN mapping rules. Write super.users with semicolons: User:kafka-broker;User:platform-admin. Remove allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true; by default only super users may touch resources without ACLs, so create the service ACLs first. kafka-acls.sh in 4.x has no --authorizer-properties; use --bootstrap-server, or --bootstrap-controller against the controllers, for example ... --add --allow-principal User:orders-svc --operation Write --topic orders.
generic: Kafka ACLs control which principals can perform operations on resources. Enable an authorizer in server.properties, define super users for administrators, and use kafka-acls.sh to grant Read, Write and Describe to each application. Follow least privilege, use prefixed ACLs for groups of topics, and audit ACLs regularly. Make sure TLS certificates are mapped to principals correctly.
note: Sources: the pinned Kafka docs do not say that kafka.security.authorizer.AclAuthorizer was removed; m1 rests on the KRaft instruction only, and the reference does not claim removal. Envelope/ClusterAction from the protocol table (lines 2028-2035) applies only to the broker principal; the mapping-rule consistency is inferred from how principals are derived, not stated. Second review: the controllers also authorize each other's quorum requests, so their own certificate principal needs the same super-user treatment; the question does not give the controllers' CN, so no point requires it and an answer that adds it is not penalised.

reference:
Two things keep RollingSync from working.

1. The feature is off. Progressive syncs must be enabled in the ApplicationSet controller; your argocd-cmd-params-cm does not set applicationsetcontroller.enable.progressive.syncs: "true", so the strategy was not applied and each Application's automated policy synced as soon as Git changed. Set it to "true" (or pass --enable-progressive-syncs / ARGOCD_APPLICATIONSET_CONTROLLER_ENABLE_PROGRESSIVE_SYNCS=true) and restart the ApplicationSet controller.
2. The steps match labels on the generated Applications, not on the cluster Secrets. Your template sets none, so no step would select anything. Add:

  template:
    metadata:
      name: 'kafka-platform-{{.name}}'
      labels:
        env: '{{index .metadata.labels "env"}}'

What happens next time:
- dev syncs first; the controller waits until it is Healthy;
- then staging, again until Healthy;
- then prod: maxUpdate: 1 updates prod-eu and prod-us one at a time;
- dr matches no step: it is excluded from the rolling sync and stays OutOfSync until someone syncs it from the CLI or UI. Add a fourth step for dr if it should follow prod.

Also expect RollingSync to force autosync off on the generated Applications (the controller logs warnings for the automated block); selfHeal no longer acts by itself and syncs come from the rollout.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Your ApplicationSet is fine as a description, but two prerequisites are missing. Progressive syncs are opt-in: your argocd-cmd-params-cm does not set applicationsetcontroller.enable.progressive.syncs; set it to "true" and restart argocd-applicationset-controller. Without it Argo CD ignores the strategy and your automated policy synced all five Applications together. Second, rollingSync steps select Applications by Application labels; put env on the template (labels: env: '{{index .metadata.labels "env"}}'). With both fixed: dev, then staging, then prod, each step only after the previous one is all Healthy; prod-eu and prod-us one at a time because of maxUpdate: 1. dr is in no step, so it is left out and must be synced by hand or given a step. RollingSync also disables autosync on the generated Applications and logs warnings about the automated policy.
generic: Progressive rollouts in Argo CD can be done with ApplicationSet strategies or with sync waves. Make sure your clusters are labeled correctly, check the ApplicationSet controller logs for errors, and use a manual sync policy for production. Consider Argo Rollouts for safer upgrades and test Kafka upgrades in staging before production.
note: Sources disagree on status: Progressive-Syncs.md calls the feature Beta since 3.3.0 (lines 4-7) and 'an experimental feature' (line 21). Whether the strategy is fully ignored or partly applied while the feature is disabled is inferred from the enabling requirement; the symptom in the question matches it.

correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Add four guards and fix one argument. (1) Reject __consumer_offsets, __transaction_state, __share_group_state, __cluster_metadata (simplest: any topic starting with "__"); the docs warn that changing them can corrupt coordinator state. (2) If keyed is true, stop and ask for approval: the default partitioner uses hash(key) % partitions, so existing keys move to other partitions and ordering per key breaks; old data stays where it is. (3) Reject add <= 0; partitions can never be reduced. (4) Compute new_total = current + add and pass that: NewPartitions(topic, new_total) takes the total count. Optionally run create_partitions(..., validate_only=True) first, then for real, waiting on each future with .result(). After success, tell the team that consumers using auto.offset.reset=latest may skip records written to the new partitions before they rebalance.
generic: Partition increases should be validated before they are applied. Check that the topic exists, that the request comes from an authorized team, and log every change for auditing. Handle exceptions from the futures, add retries with backoff, and set a reasonable timeout. Consider a maximum partition count per topic to protect the cluster.

must.text: Key each reading by meter id: records with the same key go to the same partition and are read in the order written, so per-meter order needs keying, not a partition per meter.

Rejects one partition per meter because of the per-broker partition limit from memory map areas: each partition needs at least 2 map areas against a vm.max_map_count default of about 65,535, and the docs say 50,000 partitions on one broker likely crash it.
retention.bytes is enforced per partition, not per topic: 20 TB per partition is no cap at all; a topic-wide budget has to be divided by the partition count.
Enable producer compression (compression.type such as zstd or lz4) with batching (linger.ms, batch.size): compression works on whole batches, so more batching gives a better ratio.

Computes the volume: 1.2 M / 30 s = 40,000 readings/s x 500 B = 20 MB/s; x 1,209,600 s = about 24.2 TB per copy, about 72.6 TB with RF 3, about 12.1 TB per broker before compression (10 % tolerance); a 20 TB cap would therefore cut retention below 14 days.

Names the numbers still missing: compression ratio, per-partition consumer throughput (to choose the partition count), peak or catch-up factor (meters reconnecting and replaying), and usable disk per broker with headroom.

must_not.condition: only if recommended; describing the proposal in order to reject it does not count
must_not.near_miss: Per-meter order comes from keying by meter id; a partition per meter is not needed.

must_not.condition: counts whenever stated or relied on

reference:
Not sound on either point.

Ordering: Kafka orders records within a partition, and records with the same key always go to the same partition. Use the meter id as the key; every meter's readings stay in order on a modest number of partitions.

One partition per meter does not fit a broker. 1.2 million partitions at RF 3 are 3.6 million replicas, about 600,000 per broker. Each partition needs at least two memory map areas (index and time index), against a vm.max_map_count default around 65,535; the docs warn that 50,000 partitions on one broker likely crash it with OutOfMemoryError (Map failed). File descriptors grow the same way.

The cap: retention.bytes is per partition. 20 TB per partition caps nothing. A topic budget must be divided by the partition count (20 TB / 120 partitions is about 167 GB each).

Volume: 1.2 M / 30 s = 40,000 readings/s x 500 B = 20 MB/s. Over 14 days (1,209,600 s) that is about 24.2 TB per copy, 72.6 TB with RF 3, about 12.1 TB per broker before compression; a true 20 TB cap would cut retention to about 11.5 days. Use producer compression (zstd or lz4) with linger.ms and batch.size, since compression works on whole batches; small similar readings compress well.

Missing numbers: compression ratio, consumer throughput per partition (partition count = peak rate / per-partition rate, with headroom), peak and catch-up factor after outages, and usable disk per broker.
correct_alternative: No any_of group; re-worded answer. Replace the per-meter partitions with a keyed topic: producer key = meter id, so the default partitioner keeps each meter on one partition and billing reads its readings in order. Size partitions from throughput, not meter count. The proposal would put about 600,000 partition replicas on each broker; each needs at least two map areas, far beyond the default vm.max_map_count of about 65,535 (50,000 partitions per broker already likely crash a broker). Drop the 20 TB value: retention.bytes counts per partition, so it would not limit the topic; if you want a size cap, set retention.bytes = budget / partitions. Raw volume: 40,000 msg/s, 20 MB/s, about 24.2 TB per copy for 14 days, 72.6 TB at RF 3, 12.1 TB per broker before compression. Turn on compression.type=zstd with batching. Still needed: compression ratio, per-partition consume rate, peak factor, disk per broker.
generic: Kafka can handle this scale with the right design. Choose a partition count that matches your throughput, use replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 2, enable compression, and monitor disk usage. Consider tiered storage for long retention and test with realistic load before going live.
note: No any_of: keying by meter id is the only documented ordering design here. The 50,000-partitions warning is per broker. m5 and m6 are not in the index (computed or judgement); no weight-2 point is not_indexed.

must_not.condition: only if recommended; saying it loses records does not count
must_not.near_miss: Resetting to latest skips every unread record, so it is not a way to catch up.

reference:
It will not give 120,000/s. In a consumer group each partition is read by exactly one consumer of the group, so with 24 partitions at most 24 pods work and the other 36 idle: about 48,000/s.

Numbers: at 60,000/s in and 48,000/s out the backlog grows 12,000/s; over 3 h (10,800 s) about 130 million records. After the peak, 48,000 - 15,000 = 33,000/s drains it in about 65 minutes; the oldest unread record is about 45 minutes old. If the HPA does not scale at all (12 pods, 24,000/s) the backlog is about 390 million records, the lag reaches about 4.5 hours and draining takes about 12 hours: close to the 6-hour retention.

Changes before the event:
1. Increase clickstream-raw to 48 partitions now (records have no keys, so nothing depends on the key mapping) and allow up to 48 pods; at 2,000/s each that covers 60,000/s with headroom. Run the group with auto.offset.reset=earliest first, since consumers on latest can miss records written to new partitions before they see them.
2. Retention must cover the worst case: records are deleted after retention.ms whether or not they were read. Raise retention.ms to, say, 24 h for the event.
3. Drop 'reset to latest': it throws away every unread click. If records do expire, auto.offset.reset decides where the group restarts; earliest (or by_duration) instead of the default latest.

Still to measure: per-pod peak rate, HPA reaction time, broker headroom for catch-up reads.
correct_alternative: Keep the 24 partitions and move fraud-features to a share group: share consumers cooperate on the same partitions and their number can exceed the partition count, so 30 to 40 pods can all work; the records are unkeyed and per-record order does not matter for feature extraction. A consumer group would cap you at 24 consumers, about 48,000/s, so the HPA plan does not reach 120,000/s; the backlog would grow by about 130 million records over 3 hours and drain in about an hour afterwards. Because records are deleted after retention.ms whether consumed or not, raise retention for the event well above the worst lag (several hours if scaling fails). Never reset to latest to catch up: it skips the unread clicks; set auto.offset.reset to earliest so an expired offset does not silently jump to the end. Measure the per-pod peak rate and the HPA ramp first.
generic: For traffic spikes, scale consumers horizontally with the HPA based on consumer lag, for example with KEDA. Make sure brokers have enough capacity, monitor records-lag-max, and tune max.poll.records and fetch sizes. Test the setup with a load test before Black Friday and have a runbook for high lag.
note: m2 repeats the fact of b2-10 m2 (one consumer per partition in a group); the scenario differs (burst sizing, retention, reset). Computed figures assume the 60,000/s rate starts at once and a constant per-pod rate. Share groups are a documented alternative in 4.3; no must-not catches them. Second review: the m4 alternative (share group) also echoes b2-10, whose answer is a share group for consumers beyond the partition count; here it is one member of an any_of group next to adding partitions.

reference:
Most likely the cluster CA private key was replaced this morning (for example with strimzi.io/force-replace on core-cluster-ca as an audit fix). Strimzi then generates a new cluster CA certificate for the new key and rolls the nodes; the brokers now present certificates signed by the new key. Your VM truststores contain only last year's CA certificate, so the Java clients cannot build a trust path: PKIX path building failed. In-cluster clients that read the Secret at start-up would recover after a restart.
Confirm, read-only:
- kubectl -n kafka get events.events.k8s.io --field-selector reportingController=strimzi.io/cluster-operator: look for ClusterCaCertKeyReplaced and CaCertHasOldGeneration around 10:00.
- Connect to the external bootstrap address with openssl s_client -showcerts: the CA certificate the brokers present is not the one in your truststores. A hostname mismatch would give a different error.
Fix: extract ca.crt (or ca.p12 and ca.password) from core-cluster-ca-cert, import it into every client truststore and restart the clients. During a renewal period the Secret holds more than one CA certificate; import all of them. Never distribute core-cluster-ca, which holds the private key. Do not disable verification and do not delete or re-annotate the CA Secrets.
Prevent: Strimzi does not manage external clients. Automate the truststore refresh from core-cluster-ca-cert for every renewal (validityDays 365 and renewalDays 30 by default) and agree with security that key replacements are announced and followed by the refresh.
correct_alternative: The clients reject the brokers because the brokers' certificates now chain to a different CA key. openssl s_client -showcerts against the external bootstrap address shows a CA certificate that is not the one in the VM truststores: the cluster CA key was replaced, most likely as one of the security team's audit fixes, and Strimzi issued a new CA certificate for it and rolled every node. The truststores on the VMs still hold the CA certificate exported eleven months ago. Take ca.p12 and ca.password from the Secret core-cluster-ca-cert, which contains every CA certificate currently valid (there can be more than one while a renewal is in progress), build new truststores from it, deploy them to the 14 services and restart them; ssl.truststore.type=PKCS12. Only core-cluster-ca-cert is meant for clients. For the future, the operators do not look after clients outside the cluster: add a scheduled job that compares the Secret with what the VMs trust and redeploys after each renewal or key replacement, and ask security to announce key replacements.
generic: SSL handshake errors usually mean a certificate problem. Check whether the broker certificates have expired, whether the client truststore and keystore paths and passwords are right, and whether TLS versions and cipher suites match. Look at the broker logs, make sure the clocks are synchronised, and restart the clients after correcting their configuration.
note: No any_of group; the alternative is a re-worded answer (PKCS12 route instead of PEM). Sources disagree on maintenance windows for key replacement: proc-replacing-private-keys.adoc:51 says a force-replace waits for the next window, con-maintenance-time-window-definition.adoc:25 says manual CA updates are not restricted by windows; the scenario sets no windows so no point depends on it. The kafka-restart-events runbook (indexed, not held out) corrects the documented events command to events.events.k8s.io; m4 accepts both forms.

must.text: Makes the main diagnosis: auto-rebalancing reacts only to a change of spec.replicas in an existing KafkaNodePool; creating the new pool brokers-m7 is not a scaling event, so no rebalance was started and status.autoRebalance stayed Idle.
Explains the load pattern: Kafka does not move existing partitions to new brokers by itself; new brokers only get partitions of topics created after they joined, until partitions are reassigned.
Moves existing replicas onto the new brokers with a KafkaRebalance in mode add-brokers listing brokers [12, 13, 14] (label strimzi.io/cluster: core).
Moves existing replicas onto brokers 12 to 14 with kafka-reassign-partitions.sh: a reassignment plan for the topics whose target broker list includes 12, 13 and 14, then executed.
Starts the data movement only after review: approves the add-brokers proposal once the KafkaRebalance is ProposalReady (kubectl annotate kafkarebalance <name> strimzi.io/rebalance="approve").
For the retirement, moves all replicas off nodes 3 to 11 first (a KafkaRebalance in remove-brokers mode, or a reassignment) and deletes the brokers pool only after that has completed.

must_not.text: Names a broken auto-rebalancing setup as the cause (for example a template without strimzi.io/rebalance-template: "true", or a missing add-brokers entry) and expects fixing it to rebalance onto brokers-m7.
must_not.condition: Only as the cause or the fix; describing how the template must be annotated does not count.
must_not.near_miss: The template and the autoRebalance entries are fine (they worked in August); they act only when an existing pool's replicas change.

must_not.text: Recommends deleting the old brokers pool, or lowering its replicas, before its replicas have been moved off, to push the data onto brokers-m7.
must_not.condition: Only if recommended before the replicas are moved; deleting the pool after a completed remove-brokers rebalance does not count.
must_not.near_miss: Delete the old pool only after a remove-brokers rebalance has emptied nodes 3 to 11.

reference:
Auto-rebalancing is set up correctly, but it only reacts to a scaling event, and for Strimzi a scaling event is a change of spec.replicas in an existing KafkaNodePool. That is what happened in August. Creating brokers-m7 is not a scaling event, so no auto-rebalancing KafkaRebalance was created and status.autoRebalance stayed Idle. Kafka itself never moves existing partitions to new brokers; they only receive partitions of topics created after they joined, which is exactly what you see.
Now: create a KafkaRebalance in the namespace kafka with label strimzi.io/cluster: core, spec.mode: add-brokers and spec.brokers: [12, 13, 14]. Wait for ProposalReady, review the optimizationResult (data to move, replica movements), approve with kubectl annotate kafkarebalance <name> strimzi.io/rebalance="approve" and wait for Ready. Watch disk and network on the old brokers while it runs.
Retirement: deleting a node pool does not trigger auto-rebalancing either. Before you remove the brokers pool, run a KafkaRebalance in remove-brokers mode for nodes 3 to 11, wait until it is Ready, check that the nodes hold no replicas, and only then delete the pool from Git. Do not delete or shrink the old pool first: the operator's scale-down check would block it, and forcing it risks data.
If you prefer scaling events in future, add capacity by raising replicas of an existing pool; new hardware still needs a new pool and a manual rebalance.
correct_alternative: The new pool is not a scale-up in the sense of auto-rebalancing: only changing spec.replicas of an existing KafkaNodePool triggers it, and adding or removing whole pools never does. Kafka does not redistribute old partitions on its own, so nodes 12 to 14 only got the new topics. Without Cruise Control you can move the data with kafka-reassign-partitions.sh: write the list of topics, run --generate with --broker-list including 12,13,14 (and the old brokers you want to keep), review the proposed plan, run --execute with a replication throttle, and --verify until all reassignments are complete, which also removes the throttle. For the retirement, move every replica off nodes 3 to 11 the same way (or with a remove-brokers KafkaRebalance) before the brokers pool is deleted, because deleting the pool does not rebalance anything and the operator will not remove brokers that still hold replicas.
generic: Cruise Control rebalances need time and enough metric samples. Check the Cruise Control logs and the Kafka resource status, make sure the rebalance goals are reasonable and that the new brokers are healthy and reachable. Consider triggering a full rebalance and keep an eye on disk usage on all brokers.
note: Alternative path m3b without approval, so an answer on that path misses m4 (weight 1). Kafka 4.3 cordoning (proc-automating-rebalances.adoc:20-21) applies to scale-down only; not a point. The KafkaRebalance printer columns and the Kafka status field names are from 049-Crd-kafkarebalance.yaml and appendix_crds.adoc:1985-1990.

reference:
Two things are wrong with the RBAC, and the error shows both: the request comes from system:serviceaccount:data:etl-connect and goes to the namespace db-credentials.
1. Strimzi runs the Connect pods with the service account <KafkaConnect name>-connect, here etl-connect. Your RoleBinding names a service account etl, which the pods do not use.
2. You applied the Role and RoleBinding in data. The provider reads the Secret through the Kubernetes API in the Secret's own namespace, so the access rights must be granted in db-credentials; a RoleBinding only gives rights within its namespace. The Secret can stay where it is.
Fix (least access): in db-credentials, a Role with apiGroups [""], resources [secrets], resourceNames [orders-mysql], verbs [get], and a RoleBinding to ServiceAccount etl-connect in namespace data. Delete the useless pair in data.
Check before retrying: create a SubjectAccessReview (authorization.k8s.io/v1) with spec.user system:serviceaccount:data:etl-connect and spec.resourceAttributes namespace db-credentials, verb get, resource secrets, name orders-mysql; status.allowed must be true.
Then restart the failed connector: kubectl annotate kafkaconnector orders-cdc -n data strimzi.io/restart="true" (or "includeTasks,onlyFailed"), and check that READY becomes True and the task is RUNNING. The other four connectors are not touched.
Do not grant cluster-wide read on secrets, do not mount the Secret (it cannot be mounted across namespaces anyway) and do not paste the password into the connector.
correct_alternative: The error is an authorization failure, not a Connect problem: the caller is system:serviceaccount:data:etl-connect, the service account Strimzi creates for the KafkaConnect etl, and it has no rights in db-credentials. Your Role and RoleBinding live in data and bind a service account called etl, so they never apply. Ask the database team to apply in db-credentials a Role read-orders-mysql that allows only get on the Secret orders-mysql, and a RoleBinding whose subject is kind ServiceAccount, name etl-connect, namespace data. Remove the pair in data. Verify with a SubjectAccessReview for user system:serviceaccount:data:etl-connect, verb get, resource secrets, name orders-mysql, namespace db-credentials: status.allowed must be true. Then annotate the KafkaConnector orders-cdc with strimzi.io/restart="true" so the connector starts again and resolves the placeholder.
generic: Permission errors in Kubernetes come from RBAC. Your artifact URL has no version, so the proxy now serves the new release. Its SHA-512 differs from the sha512sum you pinned in spring. Strimzi verifies the checksum before unpacking the tgz, so the build fails, which is what the build pod log shows.
Production is not affected: when a build fails, Kafka Connect is not updated; ingest-connect-0..2 keep running the previous image with the old plugin.
The first attempt did nothing because strimzi.io/force-rebuild=true is read on the Kafka Connect StrimziPodSet (ingest-connect), not on the KafkaConnect resource. Remove the annotation from the KafkaConnect.
Do not delete the sha512sum, and do not set insecure: true: Strimzi does no security scanning of downloaded artifacts, and the checksum is what guarantees that the build uses the file you checked.
Safe way:
1. Download the new release, check it (vendor checksum or signature, your scan), compute sha512sum.
2. Prefer a versioned URL (for example .../s3-sink/2.7.1/s3-sink.tgz) so the file cannot change under the checksum again.
3. Change url and sha512sum in spec.build.plugins through Git. A change to spec.build.plugins starts a new build by itself; no annotation needed.
4. When the new image is pushed, the operator restarts all three worker pods, so every connector is interrupted briefly; merge in a quiet period and check afterwards that KafkaConnect is Ready, status.connectorPlugins shows the new version and the connectors are RUNNING.
Rollback: revert the commit; that builds the old plugin again.
correct_alternative: The failing step is the checksum check. Strimzi downloads https://artifacts.example.internal/.../latest/s3-sink.tgz, which is now the vendor's new build, and compares it with the sha512sum from spring; they differ, so the image build stops and Kafka Connect is left as it was. Your three workers still run the old image, so nothing is down. The annotation on the KafkaConnect was ignored: force-rebuild is only read from the Connect StrimziPodSet. Keep the checksum. Verify the new release, compute its SHA-512, and update the artifact in spec.build.plugins with that checksum and a URL that contains the version. Editing the plugins starts the build without any annotation. When the build succeeds, the operator rolls all Connect pods, so schedule the merge when a short interruption of every connector is acceptable, then confirm the plugin version in the KafkaConnect status.
generic: Image build failures are often caused by registry access, network problems or wrong credentials. Check the push secret, the registry URL, and the build pod logs. Retry the build, and if it keeps failing, build the image in your CI pipeline instead and set spec.image.

reference:
It will not work as written, and the replication change does nothing.
Security: Strimzi configures the security of Kafka Connect itself. Keys with the prefixes security., sasl. and ssl. in spec.config are disregarded (the Cluster Operator logs a warning), so the workers would talk plaintext to the TLS port 9093 and fail. Use the dedicated fields and drop the five keys, the config provider for the password and the extra mount:
  tls:
    trustedCertificates:
      - secretName: core-cluster-ca-cert
        certificate: ca.crt
  authentication:
    type: scram-sha-512
    username: warehouse-connect
    passwordSecret:
      secretName: warehouse-connect
      password: password
Strimzi then sets SASL_SSL with SCRAM-SHA-512 for the workers' producers, consumers and admin client.
Replication: the three topics already exist with replication factor 1, and changing *.storage.replication.factor after they are created has no effect. Raise them in place: either a kafka-reassign-partitions.sh plan that lists three replicas for every partition of warehouse-connect-configs, -offsets and -status (execute, then --verify), or KafkaTopic resources for them with replicas: 3, which the Topic Operator applies through Cruise Control (Cruise Control must be deployed). Keep the settings at 3 in spec.config for future clusters. Do not delete the topics: they hold the connector configurations and source offsets.
After the merge, check that the KafkaConnect is Ready, no warning about ignored options is in the operator log, and the connectors are RUNNING.
correct_alternative: Two problems. First, the new keys under spec.config (security.protocol, sasl.mechanism, sasl.jaas.config, ssl.truststore.*) are among the options Strimzi manages, so it drops them with a warning in the Cluster Operator log; the workers would open plain connections to 9093. Configure the connection the Strimzi way: spec.tls.trustedCertificates with secretName core-cluster-ca-cert and pattern "*.crt", and spec.authentication of type scram-sha-512 with username warehouse-connect and passwordSecret pointing at the Secret warehouse-connect, key password. Second, the replication factor settings only apply when Connect creates its topics, which happened last month with 1. With Cruise Control in the Kafka resource, create KafkaTopic resources warehouse-connect-configs, -offsets and -status with spec.replicas: 3 (and their current partitions and cleanup.policy compact) and let the Topic Operator change the replication; watch status.replicasChange until it disappears.
generic: Securing Kafka Connect requires TLS and SASL settings that match the listener. Make sure the truststore contains the right CA, the JAAS configuration has the correct credentials and the KafkaUser has the needed ACLs. A replication factor of 3 is recommended for internal topics. Test the change in a staging environment first.
note: Sources disagree slightly: KafkaConnectSpec.adoc:85-95 lists bootstrap.servers, consumer/producer.interceptor.classes, listeners., plugin.path, rest., sasl., security., ssl.; appendix_crds.adoc:2088 also lists group.id, the three storage topic keys and prometheus.metrics.reporter., and exempts ssl.endpoint.identification.algorithm, ssl.cipher.suites, ssl.protocol, ssl.enabled.protocols. The Strimzi TLS example names the Secret my-cluster-cluster-cert (con-config-kafka-connect-securing-connections.adoc:47); the CA Secret is <cluster>-cluster-ca-cert (ref-certificates-and-secrets.adoc:118). Moves the replicas first with Cruise Control: after the brokers pool is ready, a KafkaRebalance with mode: remove-brokers and brokers: [0, 1, 2], run to completion.
Moves the replicas first with kafka-reassign-partitions.sh: a reassignment plan that moves every replica from nodes 0, 1 and 2 to the new brokers, executed.
Removes the broker role in a separate, later change, only after the move is complete (KafkaRebalance Ready, or no replicas left on nodes 0, 1 and 2).
Says the partition data moves from node IDs 0-2 to the new brokers' IDs (by default the next free IDs, here 3, 4 and 5), so dashboards and alert rules keyed on broker IDs 0-2 must be updated.

must_not.condition: Only as a statement about this change; describing auto-rebalancing on a replicas change of a broker pool does not count.

reference:
Not as written. Kafka does not move partitions when a node loses the broker role, and Strimzi refuses to remove the broker role from nodes that still hold replicas: the change is prevented and the Kafka resource's status.conditions show why. Merged together, the new pool would come up and combined would stay as it is, with the cluster reporting a warning.
Do it in three steps:
1. Merge only nodepool-brokers.yaml. Wait until the three new broker pods are ready; they get the next free node IDs, 3, 4 and 5.
2. Move all replicas off nodes 0, 1 and 2: a KafkaRebalance with label strimzi.io/cluster: events, spec.mode: remove-brokers, spec.brokers: [0, 1, 2]; wait for ProposalReady, check dataToMoveMB (about 2.7 TB here), approve with strimzi.io/rebalance="approve" and wait for Ready. kafka-reassign-partitions.sh with a plan moving every replica to 3, 4 and 5 also works.
3. Only when it is Ready and kafka-log-dirs.sh shows no partitions left on 0-2, merge the second commit that removes broker from combined. The nodes keep running as controllers.
The data then lives on node IDs 3-5, so update Grafana, alert rules and anything else that references broker IDs 0-2 before or with step 2. Do not use strimzi.io/skip-broker-scaledown-check to force the role change. The new brokers need room for all data (about 900 GB each of 1500Gi), which they have.
correct_alternative: The PR assumes Strimzi migrates data when the broker role goes away; it does not, and the operator blocks the role removal while nodes 0, 1 and 2 still have replicas. Split the PR. First add the brokers pool. When nodes 3, 4 and 5 are running, generate a reassignment with kafka-reassign-partitions.sh that replaces 0, 1 and 2 by 3, 4 and 5 in every partition's replica list, execute it with a replication throttle and run --verify until every partition reports completed. Then, in a second PR, change combined to roles [controller]. Because the replicas now sit on IDs 3 to 5, change the dashboards and alerts that use broker IDs 0 to 2 at the same time as the reassignment.
generic: Separating controllers and brokers is a good practice for larger clusters. Make sure the new node pool has enough resources and storage, and that Cruise Control is configured. Apply the change during a maintenance window and monitor the cluster closely afterwards.
note: Close to, but not the same family as, p2-13 (scale-down removes the highest ID) and b1-16 / b1-20 (storage shrink, pool layout): here the point is the order of a role split on a running cluster. Controller scaling (con-config-node-pool-roles.adoc:29) is deliberately not part of the scenario, to stay clear of b1-20. The dataToMoveMB figure in the reference is arithmetic (3 x 900 GB), not a point. Second review on the B1 overlap (b1-16, question overlap 0.293, containment 0.509): not a repeat. b1-16 tests that volumes cannot shrink and that data moves to a new pool (remove-brokers) or a new volume (remove-disks); here the tested facts are that removing the broker role moves nothing and is blocked while replicas remain, the order of the two commits, and the node-ID change. The remove-brokers step (m2a) is shared with b1-16 m3 and with b4-12 m5, one unit of five.

must.text: Explains the missing rows: the task has no flush(), so when Connect commits the consumer offsets it treats records that are still in the buffer, or in an asynchronous insert not yet acknowledged, as done; after a restart or rebalance they are not delivered again.
must.no_covering_set_note: no set of up to three chunks states the whole fact

must.text: Implements flush(Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> currentOffsets) so that it writes every buffered row and blocks until the warehouse has acknowledged all writes, including the inserts started asynchronously in put().
Writes the records of each put() call to the warehouse synchronously and returns only after the warehouse has acknowledged them, so no data is held between calls.
must.source: inferred from the Sink Tasks section of raw/apache-kafka/docs/kafka-connect/connector-development-guide.md (put() may buffer; flush() pushes outstanding data before the offset commit), not stated there

must.text: Obtains the ErrantRecordReporter with context.errantRecordReporter() in start() and calls reporter.report(record, e) for a record that cannot be converted, instead of only logging it, so the record reaches warehouse-dlq.
Handles a null reporter (dead letter queue not enabled) by throwing a ConnectException instead of skipping the record silently.

must_not.text: Says errors.tolerance: all with the dead letter queue settings sends exceptions caught inside the task's own code to warehouse-dlq by itself.
must_not.condition: Only as an explanation or a fix; saying that converter and transformation failures go to the dead letter queue does not count.
must_not.near_miss: The framework handles failures in converters and transformations; a failure the task catches itself must be reported with the ErrantRecordReporter.

must_not.text: Lets flush() catch a failed warehouse write and return normally (logging the error).
must_not.condition: Only in the proposed code or advice; catching to add context and then rethrowing does not count.
must_not.near_miss: flush() throws when a write fails, so the offsets are not committed and the records are delivered again.

correct_alternative: Keep it simple and synchronous: in put(), convert each record; on a conversion failure call reporter.report(record, e) when context.errantRecordReporter() (taken once in start()) is not null, otherwise throw new ConnectException("bad record", e). Then call a blocking client.bulkInsert(rows) for the rows of this put() call and return only when the warehouse has confirmed it; if the insert fails, throw a ConnectException so the task fails and the uncommitted records are delivered again after the restart. No rows are held between calls, so the default flush() has nothing to write. This costs throughput (one bulk call per put batch) but closes both gaps: offsets are only committed for rows that are in the warehouse, and bad records go to warehouse-dlq.
generic: Data loss in sink connectors is usually caused by offset handling. Make sure offsets are committed only after processing, add retries with backoff around the warehouse client, increase errors.retry.timeout, and enable errors.log.enable so problems are visible. Monitor consumer lag and the dead letter queue.

WarehouseClient and Row are the user's own classes. m2b covers a synchronous put() as an equally correct design. Second review: m2b is not_indexed (the guide implies but does not state that a synchronous put() is safe); the any_of group stays one weight-2 unit, supported through m2a's chunk.

Then: names = admin.listTopics(new ListTopicsOptions().listInternal(true)).names().get(); for each TopicDescription from admin.describeTopics(names).allTopicNames().get(), collect every partition whose p.replicas() contains one of the node IDs, print them all and exit 1 if the list is not empty. must.text: Recommends one Cluster Operator for the whole Kubernetes cluster instead of one per team: several operators, especially of different versions, conflict over cluster-scoped resources such as the CRDs and ClusterRoles even when they run in separate namespaces.
Lets that operator watch all namespaces (or a single one), not a list of the team namespaces, because watching a list of namespaces has the biggest performance cost.
Keeps one Kafka cluster per namespace: a team's staging and prod clusters go into separate namespaces, because a namespace should hold only one instance of each component type.

Lets the teams manage their own Kafka resources through the strimzi-admin and strimzi-view cluster roles, which aggregate into the admin, edit and view roles the teams already hold in their namespaces.

Keeps independence at the Kafka level: each Kafka resource sets its own spec.kafka.version among the versions the shared operator supports, so teams upgrade Kafka on their own schedule while the operator is upgraded centrally.
Treats the single operator as a shared dependency: runs it with standby replicas and leader election so reconciliation continues if the operator pod or its zone fails.

must_not.text: Endorses running several Cluster Operators on the same Kubernetes cluster (one per team, or 1.2.0 next to 1.3.1).
must_not.condition: Only if endorsed for this shared cluster; mentioning a separate Kubernetes cluster with its own operator does not count.
must_not.near_miss: A team that needs a different Strimzi version needs its own Kubernetes cluster.

must_not.text: Says that watching a list of namespaces is the best-performing watch option.
must_not.condition: Only as a performance claim.
must_not.near_miss: Watching a single namespace or all namespaces is recommended for performance.

reference:
Do not run five operators. The Strimzi CRDs and ClusterRoles are cluster-scoped, so several Cluster Operators conflict even in separate namespaces, and mixing 1.2.0 and 1.3.1 makes it worse: one set of CRDs serves everyone. Run one Cluster Operator for the Kubernetes cluster, in its own namespace, owned by the platform team.
- Watch: all namespaces (or label the team namespaces and watch all); a long list of namespaces is the slowest option.
- One Kafka cluster per namespace: staging and prod of a team go into two namespaces (team-a-staging, team-a-prod), which also gives clean names, access and recovery.
- Team control: install strimzi-admin and strimzi-view; they aggregate into admin, edit and view, so each team manages its own Kafka, KafkaNodePool, KafkaTopic and KafkaUser resources in its namespaces without cluster-wide rights.
- Independence: Strimzi upgrades become one central change, announced and tested first on a staging Kubernetes cluster. Teams keep control of their Kafka version: spec.kafka.version per cluster, any version the operator supports (Strimzi 1.3.1: 4.2.0 to 4.3.2), and they choose when to roll it. Teams that insist on Strimzi 1.2.0 need their own Kubernetes cluster.
- Resilience: the operator is now shared; run it with 2-3 replicas and leader election spread over zones, and give it enough CPU and memory for all clusters.
Numbers to settle: total brokers and resources to reconcile, how often teams need a Strimzi feature before the central upgrade, and the upgrade cadence.
correct_alternative: If the teams really need to choose their own Strimzi version, give them separate Kubernetes clusters, each with exactly one Cluster Operator; on one Kubernetes cluster, operators share the cluster-scoped CRDs and ClusterRoles and conflict. On the shared production cluster, the sound layout is one operator watching all namespaces (watching a list is the most expensive mode), run with standby replicas under leader election. Put each Kafka cluster in its own namespace, so staging and prod of a team are separate namespaces. Bind the strimzi-admin role where needed; it aggregates into the namespace admin and edit roles the teams have. Version freedom then lives in spec.kafka.version of each Kafka resource, within the operator's supported list, while the platform team upgrades Strimzi for everyone.
generic: Multi-tenancy on Kubernetes needs clear namespace boundaries, RBAC, quotas and network policies. Give each team its own namespace and resources, use GitOps for changes, monitor each cluster separately, and document an upgrade process that teams can follow.
note: No any_of group; the alternative (separate Kubernetes clusters for teams that need their own Strimzi version) is correct and triggers no must-not because n1 is scoped to one shared Kubernetes cluster. Architecture item: needs the Owner's review of the weights. The supported Kafka versions of 1.3.1 (4.2.0 to 4.3.2) come from raw/strimzi/kafka-versions.yaml, which is not in the index; they are in the reference only. Strimzi Helm chart values are not in the pinned sources; nothing rests on them. Second review: m3 and m5 raised to weight 2 (three weight-2 units: m1, m3, m5); the Owner's review of the weights of this architecture item still stands. Sources disagree on whether leader election is on by default (assembly-using-multiple-cluster-operators.adoc:10 against con-configuring-cluster-operator-leader-election.adoc:14-17); m6 does not depend on the default.

Gives each team's KafkaConnect its own build output image (a separate image or at least a separate tag).

If a shared cluster is kept with per-connector principals, restricts connector client overrides: connector.client.config.override.policy Allowlist (recommended since Kafka 4.2) instead of the default All.
Keeps database passwords in each team's own Secrets, read with KubernetesSecretConfigProvider, and lets only that team's Connect service account (<name>-connect) get them through a Role.
Names the numbers the sizing depends on: throughput and partition counts of the sink topics, connectors per team, and how long a team tolerates a connector restart.

must.text: Runs each team's KafkaConnect as the team's own KafkaUser through spec.authentication (for example type scram-sha-512 with that user's passwordSecret), so the team's connectors use the team's principal.

must_not.text: Recommends exposing the Kafka Connect REST API to the teams (for example through an Ingress) so that they manage connectors directly.
must_not.condition: Only if recommended; mentioning that the REST API exists does not count.
must_not.near_miss: Teams change connectors through KafkaConnector resources in their own namespace; REST changes would be reverted anyway.

must_not.condition: Only as a statement or a design choice.
must_not.near_miss: Each KafkaConnect needs its own image or tag.

reference:
Split the platform: one KafkaConnect per team, in the team's namespace.
- Ownership: KafkaConnector resources must live in the namespace of their KafkaConnect. With one shared cluster in connect, teams either get rights there (and see each other's connectors) or go through the platform team. Per-team clusters let teams apply their own KafkaConnector resources with the admin role they already have; with use-connector-resources, REST changes are reverted, so keep the REST API internal.
- Principals: each team cluster authenticates with the team's KafkaUser (spec.authentication) and gets its own groupId, storage topics and ACLs. In a shared cluster you would need producer./consumer.override. credentials per connector; the override policy defaults to All, and since Kafka 4.2 the advice is Allowlist with sasl.jaas.config allowed only for trusted creators.
- Plugins: in one shared image every plugin change rebuilds the image and restarts all six workers, interrupting all 45 connectors. Per team, a rebuild restarts only that team. Each KafkaConnect needs its own output image or tag.
- Secrets: use KubernetesSecretConfigProvider; each team's <name>-connect service account gets a Role on its own Secrets only. Mounting new Secrets needs a Connect restart that disrupts other connectors.
Cost: more workers in total (two per team for availability, about 12 instead of 6), six images to keep current, central templates for the platform team.
Numbers needed: MB/s and partitions per sink topic (tasks above the partition count stay idle), connectors per team, and acceptable restart time.

When processing.guarantee is exactly_once_v2 and commit.interval.ms is not set, the commit interval defaults to 100 ms instead of 30,000 ms. The aggregation's KTable record cache compacts the updates of each customer and forwards them downstream only when it is flushed, which happens at every commit or under cache pressure. The likely cause is the replication factor of the mirrored topics. MirrorMaker 2 creates each remote topic with its own replication.factor setting, whose default is 2; it does not use the source topic's 3 replicas or dr's default.replication.factor. Topic configs such as retention.ms are synced, the replication factor is not. With 2 replicas and min.insync.replicas=2, restarting a broker that holds one of them leaves one in-sync replica, so acks=all writes, from MirrorMaker 2 now and from your payment services after a failover, fail with NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS until the broker is back. dr's own topics have 3 replicas, so they keep 2 in sync.

1. In the KafkaMirrorMaker2, set sourceConnector.config replication.factor: 3, so new remote topics get 3 replicas.
2. Existing topics keep 2: raise them with a reassignment JSON that adds a third replica per partition, run kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --execute, then --verify, and confirm with kafka-topics.sh --describe.

Any broker restart that touches one of the two replicas drops the ISR to one, and acks=all producers get NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS. The three pods share one state directory. state.dir is the same path on the same NFS volume for all of them, and Kafka Streams puts the application's stores under state.dir/shipment-tracker. That directory must be unique per instance: the first pod took its lock, and the others fail in the KafkaStreams constructor with "Unable to initialize state ... multiple instances ... in the same state directory".

After the change, pods with empty directories first replay their changelogs from the earliest offset, so expect a restore before processing resumes. Verify: all three pods Running and kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group shipment-tracker --members listing three members.

Main problem: group.id has no effect in Kafka Streams. kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server ... --reset-offsets --group invoice-consumer --all-topics --to-current --export > offsets.csv
(without --execute this changes nothing) and apply them with
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server ... --reset-offsets --group invoice-agg-v2 --from-file offsets.csv --execute
or with kafka-streams-application-reset.sh --application-id invoice-agg-v2 --input-topics invoices and --from-file with a CSV of those offsets, first with --dry-run. A --to-datetime reset is safe only with a time before the oldest invoice invoice-consumer had not processed yet; the stop time itself can skip invoices if the old service had lag. Alternatively, keep the old offsets by setting application.id=invoice-consumer.

- replication.factor=1 creates single-replica changelog and repartition topics; below 3 exactly-once is effectively void. Use replication.factor=3 (or -1 with a broker default of 3) and topic.min.insync.replicas=2.

must_not.text: Says MirrorMaker 2 copies min.insync.replicas (or every topic config) from prim, so nothing needs to be set for it on dr.

reference:
Three changes.

1. Aborted transactions. MirrorMaker 2's source consumer uses the consumer default isolation.level=read_uncommitted, so records from the ledger's aborted transactions are copied to dr as ordinary records. read_committed on the DR consumers cannot help, because on dr those copies are not part of any aborted transaction. Filter at the source:

sourceConnector:
  config:
    consumer.isolation.level: read_committed

(the source connector's consumer is configured with consumer.*).

2. Durability on dr. min.insync.replicas is in MirrorMaker 2's default config.properties.exclude list, so the remote topics do not get prim's topic-level value; they fall back to dr's broker default, 1, and acks=all writes after a failover would be acknowledged by a single replica. Set min.insync.replicas: 2 in spec.kafka.config of the dr Kafka resource. Alternatively, override config.properties.exclude in sourceConnector.config with the default list minus min.insync.replicas.

3. The retention script is unnecessary. MirrorMaker 2 syncs topic configs such as retention.ms periodically (sync.topic.configs.enabled is true by default, every 600 seconds), so manual values are overwritten by the next sync anyway.

The rest is fine: replication.factor: 3 for remote topics, RF 3 for the offset-syncs and checkpoints topics, sync.group.offsets.enabled for failover.
correct_alternative:
MirrorMaker 2 must read the payments topics with read_committed, otherwise it mirrors the records of aborted transactions and the DR consumers' read_committed setting cannot tell them apart any more. Add consumer.isolation.level: read_committed to sourceConnector.config. For durability, keep MirrorMaker 2 from dropping the topic-level min.insync.replicas: by default config.properties.exclude lists it (with unclean.leader.election.enable, message.timestamp.type and the throttling and timestamp settings), so set in sourceConnector.config
config.properties.exclude: follower.replication.throttled.replicas,leader.replication.throttled.replicas,message.timestamp.difference.max.ms,log.message.timestamp.before.max.ms,log.message.timestamp.after.max.ms,message.timestamp.type,unclean.leader.election.enable
so that min.insync.replicas=2 is copied with the other topic configs. retention.ms is already synced by MirrorMaker 2 (sync.topic.configs.enabled, every 600 s), so the script can go.
generic: Make sure the KafkaMirrorMaker2 has TLS and authentication configured for both clusters and that its KafkaUser has the ACLs it needs. Use enough tasks for the number of partitions, monitor replication latency, and test a failover before relying on it. Keep the DR consumers on read_committed and check the retention of the mirrored topics regularly.
note: Two pages: the geo-replication page (read_committed for the source consumer) and mirror_source_config.html (config.properties.exclude, sync.topic.configs). That the DR consumers' read_committed does not filter mirrored records is inferred from the geo-replication recommendation; it is a must-not, not a must point. The Strimzi producers-consumers page maps the source connector's consumer to consumer.*; setting it through consumer.override.* or spec.mirrors[].source.config is not documented for this purpose and not penalised. The min.insync.replicas default of 1 is from kafka_config.html. Neighbours: p2-21 (min ISR at cluster level for ELR, Kafka on VMs) and b4-22 (replication.factor of remote topics); the facts here are different.

Returns StreamThreadExceptionResponse.SHUTDOWN_CLIENT (not SHUTDOWN_APPLICATION) for all other exceptions, so that only this client shuts down and Kubernetes restarts the pod.

correct_alternative: Use a state listener instead of polling state(): before start(), register streams.setStateListener((newState, oldState) -> healthy.set(newState != KafkaStreams.State.PENDING_ERROR && newState != KafkaStreams.State.ERROR)) with an AtomicBoolean healthy, and let /healthz answer 200 or 500 from it. Before start() also call streams.setUncaughtExceptionHandler(ex -> isRetriable(ex) ? StreamsUncaughtExceptionHandler.StreamThreadExceptionResponse.REPLACE_THREAD : StreamsUncaughtExceptionHandler.StreamThreadExceptionResponse.SHUTDOWN_CLIENT), where isRetriable walks getCause() looking for RetriableException. For SIGTERM add Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(() -> streams.close(CloseOptions.timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(50)).withGroupMembershipOperation(CloseOptions.GroupMembershipOperation.LEAVE_GROUP)))), so the member leaves the group at once and the close finishes inside the 60 s grace period before the kubelet kills the container. Do not call close() from the listener.
generic: Use a proper health check library and expose readiness and liveness endpoints. Catch exceptions in your processors so that they do not crash the stream threads, add logging around the topology, and make sure the pod has enough memory. Configure a preStop hook with a sleep so that Kubernetes waits before stopping the container, and tune session.timeout.ms for faster rebalancing.
note: Sources disagree: write-streams-app.md:185-190 still shows the Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler form; upgrade-guide.md:217-225 lists KafkaStreams#setUncaughtExceptionHandler() among the APIs removed in 4.0, and the 4.3.2 sources (KafkaStreams.java:463) have only the StreamsUncaughtExceptionHandler overload. upgrade-guide.md:364 (3.3) says CloseOptions then worked only for static groups and that the rebalance is delayed until max.poll.interval.ms; the 4.2 class org.apache.kafka.streams.CloseOptions passes LEAVE_GROUP to the consumer's close, whose javadoc (raw_catalogue/apache-kafka-api/clients/.../consumer/CloseOptions.java:30-41) says dynamic members leave; the question therefore avoids a number for the idle time.
