The deprecated KafkaStreams.CloseOptions with leaveGroup(true) still exists (deprecated since 4.2) and is not penalised. The code was not compiled.

must.text: Explains the failure: with a versioned table the join looks up the latest customer version whose timestamp is less than or equal to the order's timestamp; the only customer record is 5 seconds later than the order, so there is no match, the inner join emits nothing, and the topology works as designed.
Fixes the test by piping the customer record with a timestamp at or before the order's timestamp, using TestInputTopic#pipeInput(key, value, Instant), and keeps the versioned store.

Adds the as-of test: customer version 1 at t0 and version 2 (new address) at t0 plus 10 s, both piped before an order with timestamp t0 plus 5 s, and asserts that the enriched order carries the version-1 address.
Pipes the customer records before the order in each test, because only records on the stream side trigger the join; a table record that arrives after the order produces no output.
Reads the result from a TestOutputTopic (createOutputTopic, readKeyValue) and asserts the value, then isEmpty() to show there is no further output.
Closes the TopologyTestDriver after each test, for example in an @AfterEach method calling close().

must_not.text: Recommends switching the customers table to an unversioned store (for example persistentKeyValueStore) or dropping the versioned Materialized to make the test pass.
must_not.condition: only if recommended as the fix; explaining that an unversioned table joins with the latest record by offset does not count
must_not.near_miss: An unversioned table would join with the latest customer by offset and pass this test, but it loses the as-of semantics you want.

must_not.text: Recommends advancing the driver's wall-clock time (advanceWallClockTime) or waiting in the test to make the join fire.
must_not.condition: only as the fix
must_not.near_miss: Wall-clock time only drives wall-clock punctuations; the join depends on the records' timestamps.

correct_alternative: Nothing is wrong with the topology: a versioned table is joined by timestamp, so the order at 10:00:00 finds no customer version at or before 10:00:00, because the only one is stamped 10:00:05; the inner join emits nothing. Keep the versioned store and fix the test data instead: pipe Customer("c-17", "Old Street 1") with timestamp t0.minusSeconds(60), then the order at t0, then assert with out.readKeyValue() and out.isEmpty(). For the as-of test pipe, in this order, the customer at t0.minusSeconds(60), the changed customer ("New Road 9") at t0.plusSeconds(60), and an order at t0; readKeyValue() must return the order with "Old Street 1", and an order piped at t0.plusSeconds(120) must come out with "New Road 9". Table records go in first because only stream records trigger the join. Create the driver in @BeforeEach and call driver.close() in @AfterEach.
generic: Unit tests for Kafka Streams should use the TopologyTestDriver. Make sure the serdes are configured correctly and that the topic names in the test match the topology. Print the output topic contents to debug, check that the Customer and Order classes implement equals, and consider using an embedded Kafka cluster for integration tests of joins.
note: Pages: dsl-api.md (KStream-KTable join with versioned tables, timestamp-based semantics) and testing.md (TopologyTestDriver, TestInputTopic, TestOutputTopic). kafka-streams-test-utils is not on disk; only the API names shown in testing.md are used (createInputTopic, createOutputTopic, pipeInput(key, value, Instant), readKeyValue, isEmpty, close). Materialized.as(KeyValueBytesStoreSupplier) and Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStore(String, Duration) are in the 4.3.2 sources (Materialized.java:249, Stores.java:173). Customer, Order, their serdes and props are the team's own and invented; the code was not compiled. The grace period of versioned stream-table joins (Joined#withGracePeriod) is not needed here and is neither required nor penalised. Different family from b1-27 and b1-28 (windowing and punctuation).

must.text: Rejects relying on the mirrored changelogs: a Kafka Streams application restores its stores only from its own internal changelog topics (<application.id>-<operatorName>-<suffix>, used only by that application), so the prefixed copies MirrorMaker 2 writes on dr are not used and an instance started in B begins with empty stores.

Proposes a warm standby: run the application continuously in B against the mirrored input, so that its stores in B are already built when A is lost and failover only switches the score consumers; trade-off: a second set of pods and state, and scores computed in both regions.

Has the instance in B read the mirrored input under its prefixed name, prim.card-tx, which the default replication policy gives it on dr (so the source topic name must be configurable in the topology).
Uses IdentityReplicationPolicy for this one-way DR flow so that card-tx keeps its name on dr and the topology runs unchanged in B.
Excludes the application's internal topics (fraud-scoring-...-changelog and -repartition) from mirroring with topicsExcludePattern (topics.exclude), because the default exclusion does not match them.
Computes what a cold rebuild would need: 30 days of card-tx retained on dr, about 8 MB/s x 2,592,000 s = about 20.7 TB per copy, about 62 TB with RF 3, against the 7 days kept today. Tolerance 20 %.

Names the missing numbers the design depends on, at least the changelog restore (or reprocessing) rate per pod in B and the capacity (pods and disk) available in B, which decide whether 15 minutes can be met.

must_not.text: Relies on the mirrored changelog topics on dr (prim.fraud-scoring-...-changelog) to restore the application's state in B.
must_not.condition: only as part of the proposed failover design
must_not.near_miss: The mirrored changelogs are not read by an application in B; build the state there by running it, or by reprocessing the input.

must_not.text: Says that starting the application in B from the synced group offsets, with empty stores, yields correct 30-day aggregates.
must_not.condition: only as a claim about this plan; a design that rebuilds the state first does not count
must_not.near_miss: Synced offsets only position the input; aggregates need the state, which an instance in B must build itself.

reference:
The plan does not work. A Kafka Streams application restores state only from its own internal changelog topics, named <application.id>-<operatorName>-<suffix> on the cluster it runs against. MirrorMaker 2 writes the copies under prim.fraud-scoring-...-changelog, which an instance in B never reads, so it would start with empty stores. Starting it from the synced group offsets then gives aggregates over a few minutes instead of 30 days, and a cold rebuild needs 30 days of input: about 8 MB/s x 2,592,000 s = 20.7 TB per copy (62 TB at RF 3), while card-tx keeps 7 days, and replaying that cannot finish in 15 minutes.

Design: a warm standby. Run fraud-scoring continuously in B (on Kubernetes there, against dr) on the mirrored input, so its stores are built before A fails; at failover only the consumers of scores switch. Trade-offs: double compute and about 900 GB more local state plus changelogs on dr, and two score streams, so consumers must tolerate or deduplicate duplicates.

Naming: with the default policy the B instance reads prim.card-tx, so make the source topic configurable; or use IdentityReplicationPolicy for this one-way flow and keep B's output separate from the mirrored scores. Exclude fraud-scoring-*-changelog and -repartition with topicsExcludePattern; the default exclusion does not cover them. Do not let MirrorMaker 2 sync offsets into B's running group.

Numbers still needed: restore and reprocessing rate per pod in B, capacity in B, and the tolerated replication lag.
correct_alternative: Keep the passive design but rebuild state before it is needed is not possible within 15 minutes, so run the application in B all the time: deploy fraud-scoring in region B against dr, reading the mirrored input. Switch MirrorMaker 2 to IdentityReplicationPolicy for this one-way flow so the input keeps the name card-tx on dr and the topology needs no change, mirror only card-tx (not the internal fraud-scoring changelog and repartition topics, which the default exclusion does not catch, and not scores), and write B's scores to a separate topic such as scores-b. Its changelogs live on dr under its own application.id, which is the only place Kafka Streams restores from; the mirrored prim changelogs would not be used. Cost: a second set of pods and about 900 GB of state plus changelogs at RF 3 on dr. Still needed: restore rate per pod and capacity in B.
generic: For disaster recovery, replicate all topics with MirrorMaker 2, enable checkpoints and consumer group offset sync, and test failover regularly. Make sure the DR cluster has the same capacity as the primary, monitor replication lag, and document the failover runbook. Kafka Streams can recover its state from changelog topics, so standby replicas help reduce recovery time.
note: Architecture item; needs the Owner's review. The docs cover Streams state restoration and MirrorMaker 2 naming separately, but no page covers running a Streams application across a MirrorMaker 2 failover, so m2, m6 and m7 are inferred (m2 is the one weight-2 not_indexed point). The generic answer's last sentence is true in general but does not answer the cross-cluster question. Not penalised: a cold standby that reprocesses a longer-retained input, if the answer shows it misses 15 minutes; Strimzi's statement that offsets cannot be committed to an active target group (con-config-mirrormaker2-sync.adoc:32-34) as a reason to exclude fraud-scoring from groupsPattern. Distinct from p2-18 (MirrorMaker 2 DR for plain consumers) and b2-29 (exactly-once dedup). m6 arithmetic: 8 x 2,592,000 = 20,736,000 MB.

must.text: Sets num.standby.replicas: 1, so that every stateful task has a warm copy on another instance and failover does not wait for a full restore from the changelogs; this doubles the client-side storage.
Places each standby in another zone than its active task with rack.aware.assignment.tags=zone and client.tag.zone set to each pod's zone.
Places standbys in another zone by setting client.rack to each pod's zone, which Kafka Streams also uses to put standby tasks on a different rack than the active ones.

Cuts broker-to-client cross-zone traffic with client.rack set to the pod's zone and rack.aware.assignment.strategy set to min_traffic or balance_subtopology, which takes effect because broker.rack is set on the brokers.
Spreads the 9 pods evenly over the three zones, 3 per zone, with a topologySpreadConstraints entry on topology.kubernetes.io/zone.
Sizes local disk: 1.2 TB active plus 1.2 TB standby is about 2.4 TB over 9 pods, about 270 GB per pod before RocksDB overhead and headroom. Tolerance 20 %.

Names the missing numbers the design depends on, at least the input and changelog write rates (which drive standby and cross-zone traffic), the restore rate per pod, and the price per GB of cross-zone traffic.

must_not.text: Says standby replicas process records or add throughput (for example that one standby doubles the processing capacity).
must_not.condition: only as a statement of what standbys do
must_not.near_miss: Standby replicas are shadow copies of the state stores; only active tasks process records.

must_not.text: Keeps num.standby.replicas: 0 and relies on restoring from the changelogs after a zone loss as sufficient for the one-minute requirement.
must_not.condition: only if the answer's design keeps zero standbys for this requirement
must_not.near_miss: Without standbys a moved task blocks until its state is restored; enable standbys for high availability.

reference:
Standbys are required: with num.standby.replicas: 0, a zone loss moves a third of the tasks to pods that must restore their state from the changelogs first, which takes far longer than a minute for about 400 GB. Set num.standby.replicas: 1. It doubles local storage: 1.2 TB active plus 1.2 TB standby is about 2.4 TB, about 270 GB per pod over 9 pods before RocksDB overhead and headroom.

Put every standby in a different zone than its active task: set client.tag.zone to the pod's zone and rack.aware.assignment.tags=zone. Setting client.rack to the zone also spreads standbys across racks; tags win if both are set.

For traffic, set client.rack to the zone and rack.aware.assignment.strategy=balance_subtopology (or min_traffic): because broker.rack is set, Kafka Streams then prefers tasks whose partition leaders are in the same zone. Standbys still read changelogs across zones; that is the price of availability.

On Kubernetes: 3 pods per zone with a topologySpreadConstraints entry on topology.kubernetes.io/zone. Pass the zone into each pod, for example from the pod's topology label through the downward API where your cluster supports it, or with one StatefulSet per zone. EBS volumes are zonal, so pods of a lost zone cannot move; the 6 remaining pods must carry all active tasks, so size CPU and memory with 50 % headroom.

Still needed: input and changelog write rates, restore rate per pod, and the cross-zone price per GB.
correct_alternative: Enable one standby per task (num.standby.replicas: 1; Kafka Streams needs at least n+1 instances, 9 is plenty) so that a zone loss promotes warm copies instead of restoring from changelogs, and accept about twice the disk, roughly 2.4 TB in total or 270 GB per pod. Give each pod client.rack equal to its zone: with broker.rack set on the Strimzi brokers, rack.aware.assignment.strategy: min_traffic assigns tasks to keep consumption in-zone, and client.rack is also used to place standby tasks on a different rack than their active task, so no tags are needed. Spread the StatefulSet's pods 3 per zone with topologySpreadConstraints on topology.kubernetes.io/zone, and keep CPU headroom for the six pods that survive a zone loss. Numbers still missing: input and changelog throughput, restore rate, and the cross-zone price.
generic: Run the application with several replicas across availability zones and use persistent volumes for the state. Kafka Streams restores state from changelog topics, so data is safe if a pod fails. Use pod anti-affinity, configure resource requests and limits, and monitor consumer lag. To reduce cross-zone costs, keep the brokers and the application in the same region.
